verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." It also says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration."

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is fully open source and licensed under Apache License 2.0 (while Vault uses Business Source License 1.1).
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub API lists the pulumi/esc repo (CLI and evaluation engine) as "Apache-2.0", so the license fact is correct. Vault's LICENSE is not an OSI license (GitHub reports NOASSERTION, and the raw file starts with "L…", which fits HashiCorp's BSL 1.1 header). But calling ESC "fully open source" goes too far: the same page says ESC is a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud", and that hosted backend isn't in the Apache-licensed repo.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc --jq .license.spdx_id; gh api repos/hashicorp/vault --jq .license; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L52
verdicts.framing_note: The pulumi/esc repo is Apache 2.0, but the claim widens that to 'ESC is fully open source' when the service itself runs on proprietary Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Fully open source' clashes with the same page's 'Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud' row.

verdicts.text: Through Pulumi ESC, secrets stored in Vault can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC environments concept doc confirms two of the three properties. Environments are versioned ("Every change to an environment creates a new immutable revision") and composed by importing other environments ("values imported from other environments"). There is no feature literally called branching: the closest thing is `pulumi env clone`, described as "diff and tag versions, clone, and delete".
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Branched" is loose wording: ESC can clone and fork environments but has no branch feature. Consider saying "cloned" instead.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is a fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC get-started page says ESC "is a centralized secrets and configuration management service that is part of Pulumi Cloud" and that "ESC requires the Pulumi Cloud backend." Pulumi Cloud is the hosted SaaS at app.pulumi.com. One caveat: the pricing FAQ says "we offer a self-hosted Pulumi Cloud" in the Enterprise edition, so "fully managed SaaS" leaves out the self-hosted option.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This comparison row contrasts Vault's self-hosting option with ESC. But self-hosted Pulumi Cloud exists (Enterprise), so ESC may not be SaaS-only.

verdicts.text: Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting Vault requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say that "HCP Vault Dedicated is a fully managed implementation of Vault Enterprise," and that the HashiCorp Cloud Platform "reduces operational overhead compared to a self-managed Vault cluster." Self-managed editions (Community and Enterprise) also exist. Third-party sources describe self-hosting as having high operational complexity.
verdicts.framing_note: HashiCorp says only that the managed service reduces overhead compared with self-managed. The word 'significant' is the author's own opinion, but third-party sources back it (e.g., Infisical: "Operational complexity is high").
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Significant management overhead' is a competitive, subjective judgment. The facts behind it hold up, but the degree ('significant') can't be proven.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide a key-value store.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC environments doc says environments store named keys under `values`, and those values can be static, secret, or dynamic ("Static values are evaluated once and stored in the definition"). In practice that is a key-value store. Vault ships a well-known KV (key/value) secrets engine, but I didn't fetch a Vault source for that half in this session.
verdicts.framing_note: Only the ESC half is backed by a doc I read. The Vault KV half relies on general knowledge of Vault's KV secrets engine.

verdicts.text: Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault (it does not pull secrets from other sources).
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs describe Vault's secrets sync as one-way and outbound only: "Vault can maintain a one-way sync for KVv2 secrets into various destinations," and "Vault remains the system of records." No source showed Vault pulling or importing secrets from outside stores, which fits the claim.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says sync is one-way from Vault and Vault is the system of record. That supports "does not pull secrets from other sources," but the source doesn't directly state "can only."
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Can only" is a strong absolute. Vault's dynamic secrets engines create credentials in outside systems like AWS and databases, so reviewers may want softer wording.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC editor-enhancements launch post lists "**Auto-complete**", "**Enhanced Diagnostics**... as-you-type insights into errors", and "**Hover Documentation**". The ESC GA post lists both the "In-built Document Editor Enhancements" and a "Table Editor to support users who prefer point-and-click UI-driven method", which is the GUI.
verdicts.framing_note: Evidence is Pulumi's own launch blog posts, not product source; I couldn't check the code because GitHub search hit its rate limit. The sibling doppler.md says the same thing and also mentions IDE editing.

verdicts.text: Vault's UI offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle for editing secrets, and its editing and authoring capability is limited.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's KV v2 tutorial confirms the UI form has a JSON toggle: "Notice the JSON toggle in the UI. Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." The "limited authoring" part is a subjective comparison. A Vault issue (#6909) backs it up, noting that the JSON view is just a plain text box.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Limited editing/authoring capability" is a competitive value judgment, not a fact anyone can check; only the form-plus-JSON-toggle part can be confirmed.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference documents `pulumi env` ("Manage environments", which points to /docs/esc). Its subcommands include `pulumi env run` ("Open the environment with the given name and run a command.") for injecting values into a process, plus `pulumi env set` ("Set a value within an environment.") and `pulumi env edit` for changing values.
verdicts.framing_note: The page for `env run` wasn't opened. The claim that it injects environment variables comes from the subcommand's one-line description and the known behavior of ESC.

verdicts.text: Vault Agent's process supervisor mode injects secrets as environment variables (covering secret injection separately from the `vault` CLI).
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp docs: "Vault Agent's Process Supervisor Mode allows Vault secrets to be injected into a process via environment variables using Consul Template markup." The parenthetical about covering this separately from the `vault` CLI is the author's own comparison framing, not a claim about Vault.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide client SDKs.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC half checks out: the pulumi/esc-sdk repo has client SDKs under sdk/typescript, sdk/python, sdk/go and sdk/csharp. That Vault has client libraries is widely documented (for example, HashiCorp's official Go client, hashicorp/vault/api), but I didn't check it in this session.
verdicts.framing_note: I confirmed the ESC SDKs in product source. I didn't fetch anything to confirm Vault's SDKs, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports a declarative provider via the Pulumi Service Provider, which allows management (create, update, delete) of collections of secrets and configuration as a resource through infrastructure as code.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Service Provider has an ESC Environment resource (provider/pkg/resources/environment.go, `PulumiServiceEnvironmentResource`). It defines Create (`CreateEnvironmentWithProject`, then `UpdateEnvironmentWithRevision` with the YAML), Delete (`DeleteEnvironment`) and Diff handlers, and takes the environment's YAML (its secrets and configuration) as input. So ESC environments can be managed declaratively as IaC resources.
verdicts.framing_note: I saw the Create, Delete and Diff handlers in the part of the file I read, which was cut off; Update wasn't in that part. The Create path already calls the update API.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, hierarchical environments inherit values from the environments they import.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration." That supports the claim that an environment inherits values from the environments it imports.

verdicts.text: Vault has no equivalent concept to hierarchical, composable environments; secrets are organized by path convention and the structure is maintained by hand.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say "Everything in Vault is path-based." Namespaces are the only hierarchical structure Vault offers, and they isolate rather than compose: "there is no visibility into other namespaces regardless of its hierarchical relationship." That supports the claim that Vault has nothing like ESC's composable environments (imports and merging) and that users organize secrets by path design.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Enterprise/HCP namespaces ARE hierarchical (parent/child), just not composable/inheriting; "no equivalent concept to hierarchical" could be read as ignoring namespaces — consider softening to "no equivalent to composable environments".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC values can be either secret or plaintext, whereas Vault values can only be secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs describe KV as a store for "arbitrary secrets", and say "Secrets written to Vault are encrypted and then written to backend storage". There's no way to mark a value as non-secret or plaintext. On the ESC side, values are plaintext unless you wrap them in `fn::secret`. A third-party ESC SDK example shows that wrapper in use, but I didn't check ESC product source for this.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Only secrets" is true in the sense that Vault has no plaintext flag. But Vault KV can also hold non-sensitive config, which just gets encrypted anyway. Vault returns values in plaintext to authorized readers, so readers may take the contrast the wrong way.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC lets users see existing secrets, whereas Vault does not offer the ability to see existing secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's own Vault docs say you can read existing secrets from the CLI: "The kv get command retrieves the value from KV secrets engine at the given key name." The read command docs also say "You can use the command to read secrets." Taken literally, the claim that Vault can't show existing secrets is false. The comparison-table row may mean something narrower (e.g., a UI view or history), but the claim as written doesn't say that.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault's core job is storing and retrieving secrets, so a "can't see existing secrets" row in the table probably has a narrower meaning the doc should spell out.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated in the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration." Imports are resolved each time an environment is evaluated or opened, so a change to the imported environment reaches every environment that imports it. The one exception is an import pinned to a version tag or revision number, which the same page mentions at L95.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Automatically propagate" leaves out that an import pinned to a version won't pick up later changes.

verdicts.text: Vault has no equivalent to Pulumi ESC secret referencing; Vault has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Vault's KV engine stores secrets at paths (HashiCorp tutorial: "Creating a secret at the same path replaces the existing data"; OneUptime: KV "allows you to store arbitrary key-value pairs at specified paths"). A 2024 HashiCorp Discuss thread asking how to reference one KV value from another shows no built-in mechanism. None of the sources explicitly says Vault lacks secret referencing.
verdicts.source: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/tutorials/secrets-management/versioned-kv; https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/how-can-i-access-a-secret-from-another-secret-in-the-vault/64468; WebSearch ran query "HashiCorp Vault KV secret reference another secret path interpolation"
verdicts.intuition_flag: A flat "no equivalent" may overstate things: Vault Agent/Consul Template templates can combine values from several paths when rendering, though that happens on the client side rather than inside Vault's storage model.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC can construct new dynamic values through string interpolation, whereas Vault cannot interpolate values from other values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC half is fine. The Vault half is too absolute. Vault Agent, which ships with Vault, "configures the Vault Agent for rendering secrets to files using Consul Template markup language", and users do compose several secrets into one output this way (for example, merging secret/test1..3 with mergeMap). Vault's KV storage itself has no cross-secret references, so a qualified "Limited, client-side via Vault Agent templates" would be accurate. A bare "cannot" is not.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A flat claim that a competitor "cannot" do something. Vault Agent/consul-template interpolation is client-side, while ESC resolves values when the environment is opened, so a reviewer should decide whether the row needs a "Limited" qualifier rather than "No".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi docs confirm that ESC environments can import other environments and override only some values ("with the current values overwriting the imported environment's values where keys are redefined"). No search result describes a feature called "fork", and I did not check the claim that Vault has no branching or personal configs.
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/get-started/import-environments/; WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC fork environment override values imports"
verdicts.framing_note: Overriding values through imports is documented. "Forked for testing" may be describing imports or `esc env clone` rather than a real fork feature.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The sentence doesn't read cleanly ("without rewriting ... and overriding"). ESC has imports/composition and clone, but not a documented "fork". The blanket "Vault does not support branching" claim leaves out Vault namespaces and KV versioning.

verdicts.text: `pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault has no equivalent for comparing secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI source confirms the `pulumi env diff` half: "This command displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment." I couldn't check the Vault half ("no equivalent") in pulumi/* sources. It is plausible, since the Vault CLI has no diff command, but no Vault source confirmed it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A claim that a competitor has "no equivalent" is absolute. Vault KV v2 keeps secret versions and lets you read them, though it has no native diff. Consider softening the wording.

verdicts.text: Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp docs confirm that both named features exist. Username templating is described as "used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated," and the Transform secrets engine has its own docs and API pages. Vault has no ESC-style built-in functions for composing config values, but Vault Agent/Consul Template and VSO templating can render secrets into config files, so the "rather than" contrast is a simplification.
verdicts.framing_note: The examples named in the claim (username templating, Transform engine) both appear in Vault's official docs. The claim's negative contrast is the author's own characterization.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The Transform secrets engine is Vault Enterprise-only (ADP), and Vault Agent/VSO templating does compose secret values into config output, so "rather than functions for composing configuration values" may understate what Vault can do.

verdicts.text: Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say "Username templating are used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated," and there is a separate Transform secrets engine documentation page that describes how it transforms data. Transform is a Vault Enterprise (ADP) feature, but the claim doesn't say which edition it's in.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Transform secrets engine is Enterprise-only (ADP module); consider noting tier if the page compares editions.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Vault docs say "Audit devices are mountable devices that log requests and responses in Vault." Pulumi's ESC docs say "All ESC activities are recorded in the Pulumi Cloud audit log system."
verdicts.framing_note: Caveats the doc leaves out: Vault turns auditing off by default on new clusters, so an admin has to enable an audit device. Pulumi Cloud audit logs are only in the Essentials, Pro and Enterprise editions. Neither caveat makes the claim false.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) None of the public results confirm that ESC uses a unique encryption key for each environment. Pulumi docs say ESC secrets are "encrypted at rest and masked in output," and the per-key statement found applies to IaC stacks, not ESC environments: "For every stack Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key." No source says ESC uses TLS in transit either, though that is very likely true.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC encryption at rest unique key per environment TLS" and "Pulumi ESC FAQ \"unique encryption key\" environment"; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/concepts/environments/ ; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/support/faq/infrastructure/
verdicts.intuition_flag: The "unique key per environment" wording may have been carried over from the IaC "unique encryption key per stack" docs. Confirm it against ESC/Pulumi Cloud source.

verdicts.text: Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Security Model page says "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend." It adds that the barrier "automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is an almost word-for-word paraphrase of HashiCorp's official Security Model documentation.

verdicts.text: Each Vault cloud secrets engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint the short-lived credentials.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's AWS secrets engine API docs say "Credentials can be configured either with IAM access keys for a privileged AWS account, or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation (WIF)." Credentials can also come from IAM/ECS instance roles. Vault Enterprise supports WIF for AWS, Azure, and GCP secrets engines "without static service accounts." So a static credential is not required for every engine.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the claim says "each ... is configured with a static credential," but HashiCorp describes static root credentials as only one option, with WIF and instance-role sourcing as others.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Each" is universal, but static credentials are the traditional default, not a requirement. Suggest wording like "typically configured with a long-lived root credential (or WIF in Vault Enterprise)."

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and `pulumi-service` provider.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-service provider does ship OIDC-related resources (`provider/pkg/resources/oidc_issuer.go`, plus `environment.go` for ESC environments that use OIDC login), and ESC can be driven from the CLI, UI and SDKs. But OidcIssuer registers *external* issuers that Pulumi Cloud trusts, which is the reverse of Pulumi Cloud acting as the provider. So "from SDK, CLI, UI and pulumi-service provider" is only loosely supported.
verdicts.intuition_flag: It's unclear which surfaces "use Pulumi Cloud as an OIDC provider": the pulumi-service OidcIssuer resource configures Pulumi Cloud as a relying party, not as an issuer.

verdicts.text: Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's OIDC provider docs and tutorials only show CLI/API examples (e.g. `vault write identity/oidc/provider/my-provider ...`). None of the pages I fetched says setup is limited to the CLI, and none mentions a UI workflow either way. The claim also leaves out the HTTP API, which is documented as an alternative to the CLI.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran queries "Vault OIDC provider configure UI", "Vault 1.10 UI OIDC provider configuration applications providers keys scopes", "Vault changelog \"OIDC provider\" UI support ..."; top results (developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/identity/oidc-provider, /tutorials/auth-methods/oidc-identity-provider) didn't address UI availability
verdicts.intuition_flag: I believe the Vault web UI has had an Access → OIDC Provider section (applications, providers, keys, scopes, assignments) since about v1.11, and the HTTP API can configure it too. If so, "only available from the CLI" is probably out of date or wrong. Check the Vault 1.11 changelog/UI docs.
